title: Payment schema in PostgreSQL
idea: The schema maps Payment and Refund to tables where PostgreSQL enforces the money rules: unique keys, one success per order, and refunds never above the amount.

analogy.text: A bank ledger with printed columns. The form will not accept a refund line bigger than the deposit, whoever writes in it.
analogy.breaks: A ledger has one writer at a time; a database has many.

points: `idempotency_key` is UNIQUE, so a retried insert fails with 23505.
A partial unique index allows many failed tries but one success per order.
`CHECK` keeps refunded_minor between zero and amount_minor, whatever the code does.
Refunds lock the payment row `FOR UPDATE`, check the balance, then write.

steps.caption: Two agents refund 30000 each from P-1, a 50000 payment, at the same moment.
R-A runs `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on P-1 and gets the row lock.
R-B asks for the same row lock and must wait.
R-A sees 50000 left, inserts its refund, adds 30000 and commits. The lock is released.
R-B wakes and reads the committed row: only 20000 is left.
30000 is more than 20000, so R-B rolls back. Nothing is written.
Even a buggy code path cannot push refunded_minor past the amount: the CHECK refuses it.

code.title: Tables and constraints
code.caption: The schema on a real PostgreSQL 18, then bad writes that the database refuses by itself.

walk.text: payment: BIGINT money, TEXT enums with CHECK, a UNIQUE Idempotency-Key and a version.
A plain index serves listing the payments of one order.
Partial unique index: an order may hold only one successful payment.
Partial index for the reconciler: only PROCESSING rows, oldest first.
refund references payment and has its own unique Idempotency-Key.
Three valid rows: a success, a failed try, then a retry that succeeds.
Five bad writes; each prints the Postgres error code and the constraint.

code.title: The refund transaction
code.caption: Two parallel refunds race for one balance; then a webhook is applied twice. It uses trimmed tables so the race stays short. In a full design the refund row starts PENDING; the gateway is called after COMMIT and its answer settles the row.

walk.text: Open a transaction and lock the payment row with `FOR UPDATE`.
Refuse if the payment is not refundable or the balance is too small.
Insert the refund, add to refunded_minor, set the status and bump version.
A webhook updates only from PROCESSING: compare-and-set in one statement.
Two refunds race in parallel; print how many won, never which.
Follow-up refunds, a refund on a PROCESSING payment, and a duplicate webhook.
Final rows prove the totals and the versions.

pitfalls: Keep the gateway call outside the transaction; a row lock must not wait on the network.
Without `FOR UPDATE`, two refunds can read the same balance and both pass.
Never trust application checks alone; CHECK and UNIQUE are the last guard.

quiz.q: What does refund.mjs print for the parallel refunds?
quiz.why: R-B waits on the row lock, then reads P-1 again after R-A commits. Only 20000 is left, so R-B rolls back.

takeaway: Lock the payment row for refunds; let constraints refuse impossible money.

starters: Why a partial unique index instead of a paid flag on the order?
When would optimistic locking with version fit better than FOR UPDATE?
How should the reconciler query stuck PROCESSING payments?
